title: Longest Common Subsequence & Edit Distance
summary: The canonical 2D string DP: align two sequences cell by cell in a grid, where Longest Common Subsequence and Edit Distance are the same table shape with two different recurrences.

slides.markdown:
Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) and Edit Distance are the two problems that teach **2D string DP** — a table where the two axes are prefix lengths of two different strings, not one array indexed one way.

They matter beyond themselves: diff tools, version control merges, DNA sequence alignment, and spell-checkers all run on variants of this exact grid. Once you can build this table for LCS, Edit Distance is the same shape with three moves instead of one, and a whole family of "align two sequences" problems (longest common substring, longest palindromic subsequence) fall out of small tweaks to it.

`dp[i][j]` = the answer using the first `i` characters of string A and the first `j` characters of string B. Two independent prefix lengths, one per string — this is the shape that shows up whenever a problem compares two sequences rather than analyzing one.

For LCS specifically, `dp[i][j]` is the length of the longest subsequence common to both prefixes. The recurrence branches on whether the two prefixes' last characters match:

- If `A[i-1] == B[j-1]`: they can both extend a shared subsequence — `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1`.
- If they don't match: the best is whichever of dropping A's last character or B's last character does better — `dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])`.

slides.subTitle: Diagonal on match, best neighbor on mismatch
slides.markdown:
Picture a grid with string A's characters down the rows and string B's across the columns. A matching character pair moves the answer diagonally (up-left) with +1; a mismatch takes the max of the cell directly above and the cell directly to the left.

<<< Image: a grid with row labels being the characters of a short string A and column labels the characters of string B; show one cell where characters match, with a diagonal arrow from up-left plus 1, and one cell where they mismatch, with two arrows from above and from the left both feeding into a max() >>>

The final answer sits at the bottom-right cell, `dp[len(A)][len(B)]` — the LCS using every character of both full strings.

The table gives the LCS *length*; recovering the actual characters means walking backward from `dp[n][m]`. At each cell: if `A[i-1] == B[j-1]`, that character is part of the LCS — record it and move diagonally to `(i-1, j-1)`. Otherwise, move to whichever of `(i-1, j)` or `(i, j-1)` holds the larger value (the direction the max came from).

The walk terminates at `(0, 0)` and the characters collected, read in reverse, form one valid LCS (there can be more than one of the same maximum length — this walk finds exactly one). This mirrors the reconstruction technique from knapsack and LIS: the value table alone only gives you the number; a backward walk through the same table gives you the actual answer.

Edit Distance asks the minimum number of insert/delete/replace operations to turn string A into string B. The state is the same `dp[i][j]` — first `i` characters of A, first `j` characters of B — but now it's a **minimum cost**, and each cell has three candidate neighbors instead of two:

- **Delete** A's last character: `dp[i-1][j] + 1`
- **Insert** to match B's last character: `dp[i][j-1] + 1`
- **Replace** (or keep, if they already match): `dp[i-1][j-1] + (0 if A[i-1]==B[j-1] else 1)`

`dp[i][j] = min` of all three. Every one of the three corresponds to a real edit operation, mapped directly onto a grid neighbor — which is exactly why this problem is taught right after LCS: same grid, same neighbor cells, different arithmetic.

Unlike LCS's grid, every cell in Edit Distance has all three neighbors as live candidates every time — there's no "only diagonal on match" shortcut, because even a match still has a cost-0 diagonal option competing against insert and delete.

<<< Image: a grid identical in shape to the LCS grid, but at one cell draw three arrows converging into it — from above (delete), from the left (insert), and from the diagonal (replace or match) — each labelled with its added cost (1, 1, and 0-or-1), feeding into a min() >>>

Base cases: row 0, column `j` equals `j` (inserting `j` characters into an empty A); column 0, row `i` equals `i` (deleting all `i` characters of A to match an empty B).

| | LCS | Edit Distance |
|---|---|---|
| Question | Longest subsequence common to both | Minimum edits to transform A into B |
| Combine | max — only 2 real neighbor cases | min — 3 always-live neighbor cases |
| Match case | +1 and move diagonally | +0 and move diagonally (a 'free' move) |
| Mismatch case | Best of dropping either string's last char | Best of delete, insert, or replace |
| Base row/col | All zeros | 0, 1, 2, 3... (cost of building from nothing) |

Same grid shape, same traversal order, same off-by-one handling — but LCS optimizes for *keeping* characters while Edit Distance prices *changing* them. Recognizing this shared skeleton is what lets you derive either one under pressure instead of memorizing two unrelated recurrences.

The single most common bug in this whole problem family: mismatching the 0-indexed strings against the 1-indexed table. `dp` has size `(n+1) x (m+1)` specifically so row 0 and column 0 can represent "zero characters consumed" — but the actual string characters are accessed as `A[i-1]` and `B[j-1]`, not `A[i]` and `B[j]`, inside the loop.

Forgetting that shift causes an off-by-one that either throws an index error or, worse, silently reads the wrong character and produces a plausible-but-wrong answer. The reliable habit: always write the loop bounds as `for i in range(1, n+1)` (never starting at 0, since row/column 0 are pre-filled base cases, not cells to compute) and always index the strings with `i-1`/`j-1` inside.

Both recurrences only ever read the row directly above and the current row being built — never two rows back. That means the full `(n+1) x (m+1)` table collapses to two 1D arrays of size `m+1`: `prev_row` and `curr_row`, swapped after each outer iteration.

This takes memory from O(n·m) to O(m), which matters at real scale — comparing two 10,000-character strings needs a 100-million-cell table in the naive version versus two 10,001-element arrays optimized. The trade-off is the same one from earlier topics: reconstruction (recovering the actual LCS or edit sequence) needs the full table's history, so only apply this optimization when you're asked for the length or cost alone, not the actual alignment.

slides.sectionTitle: The same grid underneath: longest palindromic subsequence
slides.markdown:
Longest Palindromic Subsequence — the longest subsequence of a single string that reads the same forwards and backwards — is LCS applied to a string and its own reverse. Compute `LCS(s, reverse(s))`, and the result is exactly the longest palindromic subsequence.

Why this works: any subsequence common to `s` and `reverse(s)` corresponds to a subsequence of `s` that reads identically whether you traverse it forward or backward — which is the definition of a palindrome. No new algorithm is needed, just a one-line transformation feeding into the LCS you already have. This is the kind of reduction interviewers reward heavily: recognizing it signals you understand *why* LCS works, not just *how* to code it.

A subtle misunderstanding: assuming LCS returns a *contiguous run* of matching characters. It doesn't — a subsequence can skip characters freely as long as relative order is preserved. `"ace"` is a valid subsequence of `"abcde"` even though its characters aren't adjacent in the original.

The problem that *does* require contiguity — **longest common substring** — is a genuinely different problem with a different recurrence: on a mismatch, it resets to 0 instead of taking the max of neighbors, because a substring can't have a gap. Confusing the two means either solving the wrong problem outright, or over-constraining LCS's recurrence with a reset rule it was never supposed to have. If a problem statement says "substring," that's not interchangeable phrasing with "subsequence" — check which one you were actually asked for before writing the recurrence.
